method.stories: Paged through all 1,216 stories compactly (id, teller, topic, insight), shortlisted about 110 for surprise, a link to a big idea, warmth or humour, and whether they stand alone, then read every shortlisted summary in full. Episode framing and argument-style entries were dropped, retold anecdotes were collapsed to the better telling, and the final 30 were balanced across tellers (16 Amit, 14 Ajay), years (9 from 2023, 11 from 2024, 10 from 2025) and subjects, with at most two per episode, then ordered strongest first with the tone varied for reading.
method.jokes: I paged through all 2,349 items in ten chunks of about 250, built a shortlist of 88 humour and 47 reference candidates, then re-read that shortlist cold in shuffled order before picking. Jokes had to make a stranger grin without the episode, favouring the hosts' own wordplay, comebacks and self-deprecation over borrowed quips and in-jokes; references had to teach something or make an unexpected connection, not just drop a name. Lines the hosts repeat across episodes were counted once, and each list uses one item per episode, with both hosts represented.

stories.why: Declared dead in 1976 by cousins after his land, Lal Bihari spent 18 years staging his own funeral, courting arrest and contesting elections to prove he was alive, and only four of the 20,000 'dead' in his association ever came back: once the state's paper version of you splits from you, the paper wins.

A CIA plan to watch China's bomb programme from a Himalayan summit ended with a plutonium battery lost on Nanda Devi, never found, and the sanctuary shut under an environmental cover story, real history stranger than any pitch room, with the danger still up there.

Amul's clean, well-refrigerated butter flopped in Bombay until scientists added the chemicals of rancidity, because decades of Polson's poor cold chain had taught customers that butter should taste slightly off, showing that 'taste' can be a learned flaw a better product has to imitate.

Frozen before the Queen of Portugal, the Goan boy preacher Abbé Faria was saved by his father's Konkani hiss, 'Kaator re bhaaji' (they're all vegetables, cut them), a mantra that later steadied him in solitary confinement and made him a father of hypnotism: frightening moments shrink into routine work.

At Nathu La in 1967 the Chinese army blasted propaganda in Shuddh Hindi, which nobody speaks, at Jat soldiers who understood none of it, then tripled the loudspeakers because it seemed to work, a comic lesson that information warfare is only as good as its model of the audience.

A guru's dream sent the American hippie Larry Brilliant on an overnight bus to sleep at the WHO gate in Delhi, and he ended up among the leaders of India's smallpox eradication, proof that huge outcomes can turn on very odd small events.

Facing a levy that threatened Vicks VapoRub, Gurcharan Das's team refiled it as Ayurvedic within 24 hours, reached about four million outlets instead of 50,000 chemists, and shared stock so widely that every employee made a down payment on a house: Indian business nimbleness at its most delightful.

The US ran out of Fogbank, a secret aerogel for one of its own bombs, and neither today's scientists with the full archives nor the retired inventors holding their own notes could make it again, a startling demonstration that know-how lives in doing, not in documents.

When bollworms wiped out Gujarat's cotton in 2002, only farmers growing banned black-market BT seed had a crop; the state ordered it destroyed, and Sharad Joshi's farmers stood on the fields saying 'over our dead bodies' until the ban fell: a satyagraha for the freedom to plant a better seed.

The US post office's cheap universal parcel service once delivered a child, weighed at the parcel rate with the address pasted on his shirt, and posting children became normal, an absurd quirk that reveals how far a society trusted strangers.

The Dalit scholar Chandra Bhan Prasad says obese, diabetic village elders fill his heart with pride because their grandparents could never have been prosperous enough to get diabetes, a jolting reminder that the same fact reads as crisis or as hard-won mobility depending on where you stand.

Accused by an NKVD guard of passing off steel as plutonium, a Soviet physicist had him hold the metal outside at minus twenty: the guard got frostbitten earlobes, the plutonium stayed warm from radioactive decay, and the verdict was 'fine, then I'll kill you tomorrow', physics as a survival tactic under terror.

Married at nine to a 45-year-old and widowed at ten, Haimabati Sen escaped a system that pushed many child widows into prostitution, educated herself in Benares and became a doctor, a life that makes the cruelty of child widowhood concrete.

In Krish Ashok's theory, upma was born when a wartime rice shortage pushed the South towards wheat and women unwilling to spend hours on rotis chose semolina, a wheat that cooks like rice, so a 'traditional' dish turns out to be a story about war, labour and women's time.

Every intelligence agency believed Saddam had weapons of mass destruction because terrified Iraqi officials filed fictional progress reports ('next we will start killing monkeys') that leaked to the West, a chilling lesson that tyrannies lie to themselves first, so their own files cannot be trusted.

After losing a bet on Lincoln's election, Edward Weston walked from Boston to Washington and helped make pedestrianism America's biggest spectator sport for about twenty years, until it decayed into a contest of who could stay awake for six days: how a pastime done for love becomes spectacle, then something toxic.

A Berkeley professor secretly filled in Ken Thompson's graduate-school application and forged his signature because Thompson thought he was just a regular guy, a warm case for institutions that trust people to judge people, which Ajay contrasts with India's turn to rigid cutoffs.

Leaving for Karachi, the Nawab of Junagadh loaded his treasury, jewels and dogs onto a chartered plane, and when a begum cried that her child was still in the palace, he counted his dogs and told her to get off, one darkly comic scene that reveals priorities better than any treaty.

Polio left Joni Mitchell's left hand weak, so instead of quitting the guitar she invented about fifty alternative tunings to reach the chords in her head, and later said polio gave her an inner life and made her an artist, the clearest case of a constraint turning into a signature.

Spies reported about 1,500 German tanks a month, statisticians working only from the serial numbers on destroyed tanks said about 200, and postwar production records proved the statisticians right, careful reasoning about how data is generated beating insider gossip.

In 1929 Werner Forssmann, a 25-year-old doctor forbidden to try it, guided a catheter up his own arm into his heart using a mirror, lost his job and later won a Nobel Prize: a now-routine procedure began with one rebel betting his own body against the consensus.

Ajay's father had a small heart attack in 1982 that went unrecognised for a month and died of a second one at 58 in 1984, the kind of event Amit came through in 2025 with a one-hour procedure, which is what 'the miracles of modern science' mean inside a single family.

A letter signed 'Chanakya' in the Hindustan Times warned that Nehru was becoming a Caesar ringed by sycophants and urged readers to dethrone him, and years later it emerged that Nehru himself had written it, a sitting leader sounding the alarm about his own power.

The US parked German rocket scientists it could not trust, many of them diehard Nazis, in Huntsville, Alabama, a town of cows, and as their children raised local school standards it grew within a few generations into a world R&D capital, showing how talent planted in one place compounds.

When chess engines overtook the best humans, people expected the game to homogenise, but it diversified as engines exposed exceptions to old Soviet-school rules, and Anand observed that an unexpected move, probably bad in his generation, now reflects players who simply think differently: a hopeful model for tools and creativity.

After independence West Bengal cleaned up its drinking water while East Bengal did not, and cholera evolved to be milder where transmission got harder, a mind-bending case that sanitation changes a pathogen's evolutionary incentives, not just its spread.

The Lakshman Rekha, now a universal metaphor, is not in Valmiki but first appears in Krittivasa's 15th-century Bengali Ramayana, one of many regional versions in which Surpanakha is beautiful or Urmila sleeps for fourteen years, showing that the epics behave like rivers rather than fixed texts.

When Stevie Wonder refused to go on at the 1988 Mandela tribute over a missing disc, Tracy Chapman, still around with her guitar, filled in, and her album sales jumped from about 200,000 to about two million in two weeks: luck that paid off only because the craft was already there.

When Larry Page's PageRank demo found Harvard and Stanford for 'university' while Excite returned junk, the Excite executive blamed the user, saying nobody types 'university', a mistake Aravind Srinivas later caught himself about to repeat with his own mother: a confused user is feedback on the product, not a flaw in the user.

Ila Patnaik made her staff drop a paperclip in a jar before every question, and the flow of trivial interruptions fell dramatically, a tiny visible cost that changed behaviour more than any lecture could.

jokes.why: Dark irony: macroeconomic progress measured by the grade of demagogue each crash produces.
Deadpan comeback: answers a solemn rule for quiet living with its noisiest opposite.
A legal paradox in one line: the crime punished only if you fail.
Instant wordplay: splits the state's own name into three new states.
Absurd arithmetic: cut every shot of women driving and the road movie vanishes.
Self-deprecation with a point: a romantic early-death deadline postponed for lack of achievement.
Real-life absurdity: unable to get an Uber, a man books himself as a parcel.
Nails tourist hypocrisy in one self-implicating definition everyone recognises.
The free-will debate settled by its own premise; the argument proves itself.
Clean pun that also names the anxiety behind distrust of portfolio flows.
War analysis as deadpan arithmetic, with incompetence as the multiplier that evens the odds.
One question indicts a profession's standards: is 'nevertheless' two words or three?
Hospital bills as an infinite loop, then 'Zeno-phobia' turns the bad joke nerdy.
Reductio ad absurdum: evidence-based living would demand a PhD before choosing college.
Instant self-deprecation: Ajay's proud export statistic hijacked for Amit's waistline.
Inverts Acton's maxim mid-sentence; the policy wonk's dream is redrafting the Constitution.
Precise, affectionate hyperbole: twenty films in twenty years, eleven of them The Matrix.
Shows Sanskritised Hindi's stiffness by Latinising Churchill: 'combat them in the boulevards'.
Evolution recast as a social demotion, then a cheeky jab at Darwin's face.
Absurd image: bureaucratic bliss so intense that a spouse suspects an affair.
Turns a teasing compliment into a deadpan plug for his life's subject.
Absurd juxtaposition: Putin, heir to a bearded Marxist pantheon, sneers at bearded intellectuals.
Inverts the old 'what Bengal thinks today' boast into a warning for everyone else.
Policy absurdity in one line: tariffs on places without people, none on Russia.
Self-aware jab at confirmation bias: words are wise exactly when I agree.

references.why: India's rupee troubles were famous enough to be a punchline in Wilde's comedy.
A satire against women's rights unwittingly previewed Peter Singer's serious case for animals.
Biology's harmless mimics explain institutions that copy first-world form without the function.
Reframes the humble elevator as the world's busiest mass transit, explaining dense cities.
The Gita's detachment from outcomes, compressed neatly into a Spike Lee film title.
Brecht's deadpan verse skewers regimes that blame the people for failing the government.
India's quintessential wedding flower came from Mexico; many traditions are quietly imported.
A batsman's 'map of the gaps' mirrors Wald's lesson: look at what's missing.
Medieval Indian satire against caste purity, opening with a dog reciting the Vedas.
Eugenics had progressive champions too: Wells and Shaw, Fabians who inspired Nehru.
A useful German word: genius without patient 'sitting flesh' can miss the Nobel.
Debunks a famous attribution: Hemingway was six when 'baby shoes' first appeared.
Etymology links political liberalism to generosity, the sense in 'liberal with affections'.
Britain hosts, foreigners win: trusted, neutral rules attract the world's best players.
Gig apps digitise an old institution: the street-corner labour market, the naka.
